2026-10-13 | Lab 7" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg resources: - ../media/lab_07/samples.mp4 --- ## Outline - *t*-tests as linear models - Bayesian *t*-tests - MCMC diagnostics ::: {.cell} ::: # *t*-Tests as a Linear Model ## *t*-Tests as a Linear Model We can specify a *t*-test as a linear model. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Our goal with *t*-tests is to compare means. $H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ aka $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} We can estimate the overall mean of the outcome with an intercept-only model, where $\beta_0$ is the intercept. $y = \beta_0 + \epsilon$ Then, we can add a slope term $\beta_1$ to represent the difference in means between groups. $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{group} + \epsilon$ ::: :::: ## *t*-Tests as a Linear Model Together, these parameters contain us the same information as a *t*-test. For example, in an experiment, if the control group is coded $\text{group} = 0$ and the treatment group is coded $\text{group} = 1$, ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 =$ mean of control group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_1 =$ difference in means between control group and treatment group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + \beta_1 =$ mean of treatment group ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell layout-ncol="3"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.svg){width=355.2} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-2.svg){width=355.2} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-3.svg){width=355.2} ::: ::: # Bayesian *t*-Tests ## Bayesian Inference So far, we've been working with the frequentist statistical framework, Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST). :::: {.columns style="font-size:75%"} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Frequentist** In NHST, we speak only about *likelihoods*. The probability that we would have observed our data $\boldsymbol{D}$ (or more extreme data) given some null hypothesis parameter $\theta$ E.g., the probability that we would observe a mean difference on a test of $\bar{x}_\text{trt} - \bar{x}_\text{ctrl} = 5$ points given the true mean difference in the population is $\bar{x}_\text{trt} - \bar{x}_\text{ctrl} = 0$. $P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Bayesian** What we as researchers are often more interested in is the probability that a parameter $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is the true parameter given data $\boldsymbol{D}$ we have observed. E.g., given that we have observed a mean difference of $\bar{x}_\text{trt} - \bar{x}_\text{ctrl} = 5$, what is the probability that the true mean difference is $\bar{x}_\text{trt} - \bar{x}_\text{ctrl} = 0$? What is the probability that the true mean difference is $\bar{x}_\text{trt} - \bar{x}_\text{ctrl} = 5$? $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$ ::: :::: ## Bayesian Inference In order to get $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$, we need Bayes' Rule. $$ P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{ P(\boldsymbol{\theta)} P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) }{ P(\boldsymbol{D}) } $$ ::: subpoint ○ $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) =$ *posterior* distribution, this is what we want to create! ::: ::: subpoint ○ $P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) =$ *prior* distribution, information we believe about $\theta$ before seeing $D$ ::: ::: subpoint ○ $P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})=$ likelihood, the same as before ::: ::: subpoint ○ $P(\boldsymbol{D}) =$ scaling term, brings everything back down to probability scale. Makes Bayes analytic calulations mathematically challenging / impossible! ::: ::: fragment Motivates *sampling* from the posterior distribution, instead of calculating it. ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.absolute left="15.1%" bottom="-2%" width="880" height="528"} ::: ## Getting to the Posterior How can we sample from posterior distributions? We can use a *probabalistic programming language*. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ![](https://mc-stan.org/docs/img/logo_tm.png) ::: ::: {.column width="66%"} *Stan* is an open-source probabalistic programming language that's widely used to write Bayesian models. It has a well-developed, user-friendly R interface called `{rstanarm}`, which we will use! ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Means we can start to work with Bayesian models without having to learn the Stan language itself ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `{rstanarm}` R package! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("rstanarm") library(rstanarm) # options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores()) filtered_mpg <- mpg |> filter(when_any(cyl == 4, cyl == 8)) |> mutate(cyl = factor(cyl)) ``` ::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `{rstanarm}` R package! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} freq_t_test <- t.test(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg) freq_t_test ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: hwy by cyl t = 17.586, df = 144.65, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 4 and group 8 is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 9.918065 12.429731 sample estimates: mean in group 4 mean in group 8 28.80247 17.62857 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian") summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 28.8 0.4 28.2 28.8 29.4 cyl8 -11.2 0.6 -12.0 -11.2 -10.3 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 23.0 23.7 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3372 cyl8 0.0 1.0 3623 sigma 0.0 1.0 3853 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3787 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1834 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `{rstanarm}` R package! :::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"} ::: {.column width="50%"} `summary()` function contains lots of information about the model: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `Model Info`: some general information about the model and sampler (e.g., formula, number of samples from posterior, number of observations in data). ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `Estimates`: means, SDs, and quantiles (can specify with `probs`) for each parameter. ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `Fit Diagnostics`: `mean_PPD` mean of the posterior distribution of the outcome. If `mean_PPD` is very different from what you'd expect the mean of the outcome variable to be, may be an indicator of something being wrong. ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `MCMC Diagnostics`: diagnostics for the Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler (more on this later). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian") summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 5% 50% 95% (Intercept) 28.8 0.4 28.1 28.8 29.5 cyl8 -11.2 0.6 -12.2 -11.1 -10.1 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.6 4.0 4.4 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 5% 50% 95% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 22.8 23.6 24.4 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3903 cyl8 0.0 1.0 3720 sigma 0.0 1.0 3586 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3884 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1793 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `{rstanarm}` R package! :::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"} ::: {.column width="50%"} Can also convert the `summary()` into a dataframe / `tibble`. Here is an example of a 90% credible interval ($95\% - 5\% = 90\%$). ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) |> as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 9 parameter mean mcse sd `5%` `50%` `95%` n_eff Rhat 1 (Intercept) 28.8 0.00708 0.442 28.1 28.8 29.5 3903 1.000 2 cyl8 -11.2 0.0105 0.640 -12.2 -11.1 -10.1 3720 1.000 3 sigma 4.00 0.00401 0.240 3.64 3.99 4.41 3586 1.00 4 mean_PPD 23.6 0.00745 0.464 22.8 23.6 24.4 3884 1.000 5 log-posterior -429. 0.0301 1.27 -432. -429. -428. 1793 1.00 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column style="font-size:80%" width="50%"} `{rstanarm}` generally defines priors on the *z*-scale ("specified prior") and then transforms them to the scale of our variables ("adjusted prior") to actually run the model. The "adjusted prior" is what was actually used. Location and scale are another way of saying mean and variance. ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Location: mean ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Scale: variance ::: ::: :::: ## Full Model $$ \begin{aligned} \text{highway MPG}_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{cylinders}_i + \epsilon_i && \text{likelihood: a linear model} \\ \beta_0 &\sim \text{Normal}(24, 17) && \text{prior for intercept} \\ \beta_1 &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 34) && \text{prior for slope} \\ \sigma_\epsilon &\sim \text{Exponential}(0.15) && \text{prior for residual variance} \end{aligned} $$

::: {.callout-note style="font-size:80%"} ### Note Normal distributions are specified here as $\text{Normal}(\text{mean}, \ \text{SD})$ not $\text{Normal}(\text{mean}, \ \text{variance})$. ::: ## Changing Priors :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Original Model** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column style="font-size:80%" width="50%"} **Changing Priors** `{rstanarm}` generally defines priors on the *z*-scale ("specified prior") and then transforms them to the scale of our variables ("adjusted prior") to actually run the model. The "adjusted prior" is what was actually used. Location and scale are another way of saying mean and variance. We can choose to specify a prior on the *z*-scale (`autoscale = T`) or as-is (default) (example on next slide). ::: :::: ## Changing Priors :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Original Model** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Changing Priors** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, prior_intercept = normal(24, 12), prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T), family = "gaussian" ) ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size:80%"} With these priors, we're saying... ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Intercept ($\beta_0$): Four-cylinder cars probably get around 24 highway MPG, and we’re ~95% sure it’s within $24 \pm 2 \times 12 = [0, 48]$ (understanding prior density based on $\pm 2 \ \text{SD} \approx 95\%$ of the distribution shorthand). ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Slope ($\beta_1$): Centered on zero because eight-cylinder cars may be better or worse. The SD of 1.5 is in standardized units (`autoscale` converts it to MPG). ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Changing Priors :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Original Model** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Changing Priors** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, prior_intercept = normal(24, 12), prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T), family = "gaussian" ) summary(bayes_t_test_v2, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 5% 50% 95% (Intercept) 28.8 0.5 28.0 28.8 29.5 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.3 -11.1 -10.1 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.6 4.0 4.4 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 5% 50% 95% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 22.9 23.6 24.4 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3886 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4071 sigma 0.0 1.0 3672 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 4199 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1798 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Visualizing Results The `bayesplot` package provides many helpful functions for plotting results of a Bayesian model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bayesplot") library(bayesplot) ``` ::: ## Visualizing Results :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} We can check how well our observed data ($y$) compare to the fitted model's predictions ($y_{rep}$). ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayesplot::ppc_violin_grouped( y = filtered_mpg$hwy, yrep = posterior_predict(bayes_t_test_v2, draws = 50), group = filtered_mpg$cyl ) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Visualizing Results :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} We can check how well our observed data ($y$) compare to the fitted model's predictions ($y_{rep}$). Diagnostics Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta}) P(\boldsymbol{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. But most of the time, $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models by drawing **samples** from the posterior with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-37-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Diagnostics with Bayes But most of the time, $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). [The job of MCMC is to explore and sample from the posterior probability distribution $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$ for all $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ at a rate proportional to each $\boldsymbol{\theta}$'s probability.]{.fragment} [So, after many MCMC samples, we end up with a density distribution of samples with height matching $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$, and we can use those samples to make inferences about our parameters and outcomes!]{.fragment} ::: {.subpoint .fragment} ○ E.g., we believe there is a 90% chance the difference in highway MPG between four- and eight-cylinder cars is within the interval [-12.25, -10.08]. ::: [But, all this hinges on the MCMC sampler---we have to check it for evidence that it *sampled well*.]{.fragment} ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} [This is called a *trace plot*. It shows the samplers' samples for each iteration it runs. Can you tell if this sampler sampled well?]{.fragment fragment-index=2} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index=1} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-38-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scale_colors <- c("steelblue", "#D98282", "#6BAE9D", "#8C7AAE") x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} What if I told you we ran another, completely separate run, and its samples looked like this? ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 2, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) + guides(color = guide_none()) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Or a third? How much confidence do you have in the sampler now? [Looking at traceplots cannot guarantee the sampler is **correctly** sampling from the distribution, but if we run multiple *chains* (separate runs of MCMC, each doing their own thing independently), we can at least check if the sampler is sampling **consistently**.]{.fragment} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-44-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 4, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) + guides(color = guide_none()) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Our example's trace plots! Also from `bayesplot`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayesplot::mcmc_trace(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-46-1.svg){width=1152} ::: ::: [Good! They look like "fuzzy caterpillars."]{.fragment} [What does a bad chain look like?]{.fragment} ## Bad Sampling Example Messing with the algorithm on purpose to make it sample poorly... :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="90%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-47-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_example <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, seed = 12345, chains = 4, iter = 1200, warmup = 200, adapt_delta = 0.7, control = list( max_treedepth = 2 ) ) mcmc_trace(bad_example) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} [Ick!]{.fragment} ::: :::: ## Rhat Looking at traceplots is great, but it's also helpful to have a numerical measure of how well the chains mixed. Especially when you have lots of parameters, not just three. [Rhat ($\hat{R}$, read "R-hat") is a measure of convergence among different MCMC *chains*.]{.fragment} [The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains.]{.fragment} ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-49-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-50-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-51-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-52-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="30%"} Variance between chain means is sooo different from variance within chains! ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-53-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-54-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-55-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="30%"} Variance between chain means is very close to variance within chains! ::: :::: ## Rhat In practice, you want to see $\hat{R}$ values less than 1.01. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 28.8 0.5 28.2 28.8 29.4 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.0 -11.1 -10.3 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 23.0 23.6 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3886 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4071 sigma 0.0 1.0 3672 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 4199 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1798 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) |> as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |> select(parameter, Rhat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 parameter Rhat 1 (Intercept) 1.000 2 cyl8 1.000 3 sigma 1.00 4 mean_PPD 1.000 5 log-posterior 1.00 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment All of our $\hat{R}$ values were less than $1.01$. ::: ::: :::: ## Effective Sample Size (ESS) In order to closely approximate the posterior ($P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})$, the point of this all!), we need to make sure we have a large number of MCMC samples. But one issue: the samples within a chain are **not** independent samples. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-58-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="66%"} Do you see how they follow each other around? ESS accounts for that *autocorrelation*. No hard and fast rule, but might be concerned if ESS is lower than 400 or lower than 10% of your total samples. ::: :::: ## Effective Sample Size (ESS) Let's check our ESS values. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 28.8 0.5 28.2 28.8 29.4 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.0 -11.1 -10.3 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 23.0 23.6 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3886 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4071 sigma 0.0 1.0 3672 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 4199 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1798 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) |> as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |> select(parameter, n_eff) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 parameter n_eff 1 (Intercept) 3903 2 cyl8 3720 3 sigma 3586 4 mean_PPD 3884 5 log-posterior 1793 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment All of our ESS values were large, with the lowest being $n_\text{eff} = 1932$. ::: ::: :::: ## Warnings ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_example <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, seed = 12345, iter = 40) ``` ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-64-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc_trace(bad_example) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Output** ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1: There were 4 chains where the estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information was low. See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bfmi-low 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems 3: The largest R-hat is 1.83, indicating chains have not mixed. Running the chains for more iterations may help. See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#r-hat 4: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable. Running the chains for more iterations may help. See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bulk-ess 5: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable. Running the chains for more iterations may help. See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#tail-ess 6: Markov chains did not converge! Do not analyze results! ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Warnings [Stan documentation on warnings](https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/diagnostics-warnings.html){preview-link="true"} [`{rstanarm}` documentation on troubleshooting](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/articles/rstanarm.html#troubleshooting){preview-link="true"} Things to try... :::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Rhat or ESS too low?** Try increasing the number of samples (`iter`, default is 1000 for each of four chains). ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Divergent transitions?** Increase `adapt_delta` towards 1 (default is `0.95`) ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Max treedepth exceeded?** If everything else is good, probably fine. Otherwise, try increasing `max_treedepth` (default is 15). Add to `control` argument (`control = list(max_treedepth = 16)`). ::: :::: ## Diagnostics TLDR :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Rhat** Want $\hat{R} < 1.01$ for all parameters.
::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **ESS** Want ESS > 400ish for all parameters.
::: :::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Trace Plots** Want trace plots to look like "fuzzy caterpillars" for all parameters. All overlapping, none of the chains higher or lower on average than others. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Warnings** Try to adjust the sampler if you encounter any warnings. Check for bugs in your formula syntax, increase `iter`, etc. If you can't get the warning to go away, make sure to mention it in your writeup. ::: :::: ## Bayes Factors Comparing models to each other. Here, an intercept-only model to a slope-and-intercept model. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bridgesampling") library(bayestestR) bayes_t_test_v0 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ 1, data = filtered_mpg, prior_intercept = normal(24, 12), family = "gaussian", diagnostic_file = here::here("lab", "model-diagnostics", "bayes_t_test_v0.csv") ) bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T), prior_intercept = normal(24, 12), family = "gaussian", diagnostic_file = here::here("lab", "model-diagnostics", "bayes_t_test_v2.csv") ) bayes_factor <- bayesfactor_models(bayes_t_test_v0, bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_factor ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bayes Factors for Model Comparison Model BF [2] cyl 9.43e+33 * Against Denominator: [1] (Intercept only) * Bayes Factor Type: marginal likelihoods (bridgesampling) ``` ::: ::: We can say the model with the slope term is $9.44\times10^{33}$ (very large!) times as likely as the model without. ::: :::: ## Lab 07 Assignment Due **Friday**, 10/16!

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
